## Literate Programming

**Literate programming** is a paradigm introduced by Donald Knuth.

It mixes computer code with a description of its function in natural language
(such as English), along with macros, from which compilable source code can be
generated.

Since 2010, literate programming has grown rapidly with notebook interfaces.
Modern examples include **Jupyter Notebook** and **R Notebooks**.

---

## What is an R Notebook?

An **R Notebook** is a plain-text file with the extension `.Rmd`. When you open
it in RStudio, it becomes a notebook interface for R.

- They consist of **code chunks** that can be executed independently and
  interactively, with output visible immediately beneath the input.
- R Notebooks are written in **R Markdown**.
- Notebooks can be **published by knitting** them into a variety of formats:
  HTML, PDF, Word, dashboard, Shiny apps, and more.


---

## Elements of R Markdown

R Markdown (and notebooks) consists of three main elements:

1. **YAML metadata**
2. **Text**
3. **Code chunks**

Let's start by exploring each one in this file now...

---

## 1. YAML Metadata

We place the metadata at the top of the document between three pairs of dashes
`---`. The syntax is **YAML** (YAML Ain't Markup Language).

Look at the YAML block at the very top of this file:

```yaml
---
title: "My first markdown"
author: "Your name here"
date: "2023-03-09"
output: html_document
---
```

Note — **YAML uses Python-style indentation** (spaces, not tabs).

To see all available options for a format, use the R help page:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
?rmarkdown::html_document
```

Output formats are often accompanied by several format options:

```yaml
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true        # Add a table of contents
    toc_depth: 2     # Include headings up to level 2
    dev: 'svg'       # Use SVG graphics device
```

---

## 2. Text — Markdown Syntax

The body of the document follows the metadata. The syntax for text is Markdown.

### Inline formatting

| Markdown              | Output                  |
|-----------------------|-------------------------|
| `*italics*`           | *italics*               |
| `**bold**`            | **bold**                |
| `sub~script~`         | sub~script~             |
| `super^script^`       | super^script^           |
| `` `code` ``          | `code`                  |
| `[text](link)`        | [text](https://example.com) |
| `![](path/image.png)` | *(embeds an image)*     |
| `text^[footnote]`     | text^[adds a page footnote] |

Complete list: <https://www.rstudio.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/rmarkdown-reference.pdf>

### Block-level elements

| Markdown                   | Output                        |
|----------------------------|-------------------------------|
| `# Header`                 | Level 1 heading (largest)     |
| `## Header`                | Level 2 heading               |
| `### Header`               | Level 3 heading               |
| `- item` / `- item`        | Unordered bullet list         |
| `1. item` / `2. item`      | Ordered numbered list         |

**Blockquote** — prefix lines with `>`:

> "Wise men talk because they have something to say; fools, because they have
> to say something"
>
> Plato

**Plain code block** — wrap text in triple backticks (no `{r}`) to display it
as formatted code without executing it:

```
this is some R code dim(d)
```

---

## 3. Code Chunks


You can insert a new R code chunk with **Cmd+Option+I** (Mac) or **Ctrl+Alt+I**
(Windows/Linux).

You can do many things in a code chunk: produce **text output**, **tables**, or
**graphics**.

You have control over these outputs with **chunk options**, provided between
` ```{r ` and `}`. For example, the following chunk hides text output:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Chunk options go in the header line, after the chunk label:
# ```{r chunk-label, results='hide'}
```

**Chunk labels** are mainly used in filenames of plots and cache.
They can also be used to indicate chunk role.

Here is a live example — run this chunk now with **Ctrl+Shift+Enter**:

```{r first-chunk}
# A basic computation — result appears below
mean(mpg$hwy)
```

```{r first-plot}
# A plot — appears inline below this chunk when you run it
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, colour = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title  = "Engine Displacement vs Highway MPG",
       x      = "Displacement (L)",
       y      = "Highway MPG",
       colour = "Car Class") +
  theme_bw()
```

**Shortcuts:**

| Action           | Windows / Linux    | Mac              |
|------------------|--------------------|------------------|
| Insert chunk     | `Ctrl+Alt+I`       | `Cmd+Option+I`   |
| Run current chunk | `Ctrl+Shift+Enter` | `Cmd+Shift+Enter`|
| Knit document    | `Ctrl+Shift+K`     | `Cmd+Shift+K`    |

---

## Chunk Options

### `echo` — show the code or not?

`echo = FALSE` runs the code and shows only the **output** — the code itself
is hidden. Useful for clean reports where readers only care about results.

```{r echo-demo, echo = FALSE}
# Reader sees only this output, not the code
summary(mpg[, c("displ", "hwy", "cty")])
```

### `include` — run silently, show nothing

`include = FALSE` runs the code but hides **everything** — no code, no output,
no messages. This is what the setup chunk at the top uses.

```{r silent-calc, include = FALSE}
# This runs and stores objects, but nothing appears in the document
n_cars   <- nrow(mpg)
mean_hwy <- round(mean(mpg$hwy), 1)
max_hwy  <- max(mpg$hwy)
```

The values computed above (`n_cars`, `mean_hwy`, `max_hwy`) are now available
for use in inline R code later in this document.

### `fig.width` and `fig.height`

Control the plot size **in inches**. Default is `fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5`.

```{r wide-plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 3}
# A wide, short figure — note the chunk header: fig.width=10, fig.height=3
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = manufacturer, y = hwy)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Highway MPG by Manufacturer", x = NULL, y = "Highway MPG") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

### `fig.cap` — add a caption to figures

`fig.cap = "..."` adds a caption below graphical output:

```{r caption-demo, fig.cap = "Figure 1. Petal length vs petal width, coloured by species.", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Petal.Length, y = Petal.Width, colour = Species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Petal Length (cm)", y = "Petal Width (cm)") +
  theme_bw()
```

### `warning`, `message`, and `error` — suppress R noise

Whether to show warnings, messages, and errors in the output document.

- `warning = FALSE` suppresses warning messages.
- `message = FALSE` suppresses informational messages (e.g. from `library()`).
- Both are set globally in the setup chunk at the top of this file.

### `cache` — skip re-running expensive chunks

`cache = TRUE` saves the chunk's result on first run. On subsequent knits, the
chunk is **skipped** and the saved result is reused — saving time for slow
computations.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Example: a slow computation you don't want to re-run every time
# ```{r slow-model, cache = TRUE}
# big_model <- lm(hwy ~ ., data = mpg)
# ```
```

Many more options at: <https://yihui.org/knitr/options/#chunk-options>

---

## Global Chunk Options

If a certain option needs to be frequently set in multiple chunks, set it
**globally** in the first code chunk of your document:

```{r global-opts-demo, eval = FALSE}
# Place this in your setup chunk:
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 8, collapse = TRUE)
```

Individual chunks can still **override** a global default by specifying the
option locally in their own header.

Look at the setup chunk at the top of this file — it sets `echo = TRUE`,
`warning = FALSE`, and `message = FALSE` for the whole document.

## R Notebooks

An **R Notebook** is an R Markdown document with chunks that can be executed
independently and interactively, with output visible immediately beneath the input.

- Any R Markdown document can be used as a notebook, and all R Notebooks can be
  rendered to other R Markdown document types.
- A notebook can therefore be thought of as a **special execution mode** for
  R Markdown documents.
- Notebooks are a good choice **while authoring** the document and iterating
  on code.

### Creating a notebook

You can create a new notebook from the menu:
**File > New File > R Notebook**.

You can also take an existing R Markdown doc and set the output to
`html_notebook` in the YAML metadata:

```yaml
---
title: "My Notebook"
output: html_notebook
---
```

### Use code chunks effectively

As a chunk's output appears beneath the chunk, it is helpful to **split chunks
that produce multiple outputs** into two or more chunks which each produce only
one output.

To do this, select the code to split, then use the new chunk keyboard shortcut
(**Cmd+Option+I**, or **Ctrl+Alt+I**).
